_: spanish-sounds.json — the table behind decks/Spanish-Alphabet-and-Pronunciation.folio-deck.json, read by build-spanish-sounds.js. Every IPA value, every `when` and every sentence in `like` and `says` is taken from the Wikipedia article named in `source` at the revision given (CC BY-SA 4.0): the tables 'Consonants', 'Vowels' and 'Semivowels' under 'Letter-to-sound correspondences', and the sections 'Stress and accentuation', 'Differential accents' and 'Punctuation'. Wiki markup is turned into <b> and <i> and ⟨ ⟩, a link becomes its text, a footnote is dropped, a cut inside a passage is marked […], and nothing is reworded. `rx` is NOT from the article: it is how the builder finds, among the DELE A1 deck's headwords (each tested as it is said, lower case with the space after an article taken out), the words that show a row; a row no A1 headword shows is not carded, and a letter none of whose rows is shown has no card. `words` and `sentences` name DELE A1 cards and their example sentences; the builder refuses one the deck does not carry. Example words are NOT in this file: each is a shipped A1 card, with that card's meaning and speaker. A row's `key` is what spanish-ids.json pins its card id to — never rename one.

rules.name: a word ending in a vowel, n or s
rules.says: The default stress is on the penultimate (next-to-last) syllable on words that end in a vowel, ⟨n⟩ or ⟨s⟩ (not preceded by another consonant) […].

rules.name: a word ending in another consonant
rules.says: The default stress is […] on the final syllable when the word ends in any consonant other than ⟨n⟩ or ⟨s⟩ or in a consonant group.

rules.name: the acute accent
rules.says: Words that do not follow the default stress have an acute accent over the stressed vowel. In many cases, the accent is essential to understanding what a word means, for example hablo ‘I speak’ contrasts with habló ‘he/she/you spoke’.

rules.name: one-syllable words told apart by the accent
rules.says: In eight cases, the written accent is used to distinguish stressed monosyllabic words from clitics:
pairs: dé ('give' or present subjunctive and imperative of 'dar')

rules.name: question words
rules.says: The written accent is also used in the interrogative pronouns to distinguish them from relative pronouns (which are pronounced the same but unstressed):

rules.name: the inverted marks
rules.says: Spanish has the unusual feature of indicating the beginning of an interrogative or exclamatory sentence or phrase with inverted variants of the question mark and exclamation mark (¿ and ¡), respectively. […] These inverted forms appear additionally at the beginning of these sentences or clauses. For example, the English phrase "How old are you?" has just the final question mark, while the Spanish equivalent, ¿Cuántos años tienes? begins with an inverted question mark.
